query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiAl single-phase HEA, the incorporation of aluminum facilitates the rapid formation of a continuous, submicron-thick (≈1 μm) Al2O3-rich protective oxide layer that persists above 900 °C, while a CrFeCoNiMn baseline instead forms thicker, porous, and unstable Mn-rich oxide scales that are prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, single-phase CrFeCoNiX HEA with X = Al or Mn, produced by arc-melting and homogenized to ensure uniform composition as confirmed by XRD.
generation.intervention: Expose polished samples to an oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., 20% O2 in N2) at 900–1100 °C for 24 hours.
generation.conditions: Exposure at temperatures greater than 900 °C; constant oxygen partial pressure; identical duration; samples must remain in a single-phase, homogeneous solid-solution state during treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a coherent, continuous Al2O3 layer with a thickness of approximately 1 μm at the metal/oxide interface provides an effective diffusion barrier, while Mn-rich alloys yield multi-layered, porous oxide scales with interfacial voids and cracks.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum’s lower oxygen permeability and relatively slower cation diffusivity compared to manganese lead to the rapid nucleation of a stable Al2O3 layer that adheres firmly to the substrate. In contrast, the high diffusivity of Mn results in excessive outward migration, pore formation, and the development of unstable, thick oxide scales that spall off under thermal stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-containing alloy will manifest a thin, uniform, and adherent oxide scale (around 1 μm thick) with minimal spallation, whereas the Mn-containing alloy will display a significantly thicker (potentially 5–10 times greater), porous, cracked, and unstable oxide scale under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNiMn alloy tested under identical oxidation conditions.
generation.boundary: Applicable to single-phase HEAs exposed at 900–1100 °C in moderate oxygen partial pressure environments, assuming negligible secondary phase formation during oxidation.
generation.uncertainty: Local compositional variations, minor elemental segregation, or slight deviations in diffusion coefficients could affect the exact oxide scale thickness and stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiX alloys, one with Al and one with Mn, ensuring homogeneous single-phase microstructures. Oxidize both sets in a 20% O2/N2 atmosphere at 950 °C for 24 hours. Perform cross-sectional SEM/TEM and XPS analyses to determine oxide phase composition, thickness, and adhesion.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and continuity determined by cross-sectional imaging.
Phase identification of oxide scales via XRD and XPS.
Mechanical adhesion/spallation tests to assess oxide stability.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not produce a significantly thinner, more coherent, and adherent Al2O3-rich oxide layer compared to the thicker, porous Mn-rich oxide scale, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, or Fe3O4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. cited_evidence.text: In the case of the Mn15Al5 alloy, the outer part of the oxide layer was mainly composed of Mn, suggesting the presence of MnxOy oxides followed by a thin layer of Cr-based oxides found at the metal/oxide interface. Moreover, a significant level of porosity was found within its closest proximity of it. The overall thickness of the whole layer after 100 h annealing reached approximately 25 µm. More importantly, the Mn15Al5 alloy was the only one showing strong sub-surface oxidation and developed internal porosity due to the diffusion of Mn toward the oxide layer. It was found that the sub-surface porosity reached up to ≈100 µm into the alloy core and likely may further progress with the increasing time of annealing. papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMn-based high-entropy alloys (with extensions to systems incorporating Al)
papers.approach: Combined in situ atom probe tomography, high-resolution electron microscopy, XRD, and XANES in controlled oxygen environments at high temperatures (900–1100 °C)
papers.findings: Identified formation of layered oxide scales where fast‐diffusing elements (e.g., Cr and Mn) segregate to form distinct oxide sub-layers. Under certain conditions, formation of a coherent inner Cr-rich layer coexists with an outer Mn-rich layer that may spall; the introduction of Al can promote formation of a thin, protective alumina layer.
papers.mechanism: Proposes an interplay of element-specific oxidation potentials and diffusion rates (characterized by the preferential interactivity parameter, PIP) that control whether a stable, coherent oxide (e.g., protecting Cr2O3 or Al2O3) forms versus an unstable multilayer that cracks or spalls. The balance between cation outward diffusion and oxygen inward diffusion, modified by local composition and interface stress (as seen in the Thermo-Oxidative Composition Inversion or TOCI effect), governs the outcome.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Insights into the Oxidation Mechanisms of CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy Using In Situ X-ray Diffraction.
papers.approach: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) experiments in air, tracking phase evolution from 500 °C to 1100 °C
papers.findings: Observed formation of non-protective, graded oxide layers with initial Mn2O3 and switching to Mn3O4 at higher temperatures. A layered structure formed, but notably a protective Cr2O3 scale was absent, with Mn depletion from the alloy noted.
papers.mechanism: Suggests that differential diffusion rates, especially the high mobility of Mn relative to Cr and other species, result in an unstable outer oxide formation that fails to protect the substrate from further oxidation.

papers.title: Influence of the Al Content on the Properties of Mechanically Alloyed CoCrFeNiMnXAl20-X High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMnXAl20-X high-entropy alloys (with variable X = Mn substitution by Al)
papers.approach: Mechanical alloying with controlled substitutions of Mn by Al followed by thermal oxidation studies at high temperatures
papers.findings: Alloys with higher Al content shift the oxidation behavior from forming Mn-dominated, porous and unstable oxide scales to developing thin, coherent, Al-based oxide layers that are protective against further oxidation.
papers.mechanism: Highlights the role of Al in promoting the formation of stable Al2O3 by reducing the effective diffusion of oxygen and metal cations, thus enabling a more coherent protective layer. The baseline comparison is against alloys with low Al (e.g., Mn15Al5), which develop extensive porosity and sub-surface oxidation.

papers.title: Modeling Oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Using Stochastic Cellular Automata.
papers.approach: Computational mesoscale modeling using stochastic cellular automata informed by molecular simulation diffusion coefficients; simulations included both single-crystal and dendritic (multiphasic) microstructures
papers.findings: Reproduced parabolic oxidation kinetics and demonstrated that the microstructural distribution (homogeneous versus phase-separated) influences whether protective oxides (α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3) form uniformly or segregate into non-uniform clusters.
papers.mechanism: Argues that both bulk and grain-boundary diffusion processes control the kinetics of oxide formation. Microstructural features (e.g., dendritic segregation) affect local oxygen diffusion and cation migration, which in turn determine the scale’s integrity and adherence.

papers.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with ultrafine-grained microstructure
papers.approach: Surface deformation techniques (e.g., shot peening, UNSM) to produce ultrafine grains followed by oxidation tests at 900–1050 °C
papers.findings: Ultrafine-grained samples demonstrated improved oxidation resistance with the formation of a uniform, coherent, Cr-rich oxide scale that inhibited further oxidation, as evidenced by reduced oxide scale thickness and increased activation energy for oxidation.
papers.mechanism: Proposes that a high density of grain boundaries accelerates Cr cation diffusion, enabling rapid formation of a continuous and protective oxide layer. Enhanced intergranular diffusion reduces the likelihood of scale cracking or spallation.

papers.title: High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of an Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Oxidation experiments at 700 °C and 900 °C using 3D laser printed specimens, with phase identification by XRD and surface morphology analysis
papers.findings: At 900 °C, the alloy developed a spinel-type, multi-component oxide layer that exhibited poor adhesion and spallation. The process was accompanied by Kirkendall porosity and a marked degradation in oxidation resistance.
papers.mechanism: At high temperatures, differential diffusion (with Cr, Mn, and Fe diffusing faster than Co) promotes the formation of unstable, porous oxides that lead to rapid spallation. The absence of a stabilizing Ni component reduces the likelihood of forming a continuous, protective Cr2O3 scale.

established: Diffusion rates and oxidation potentials of individual elements (Cr, Mn, Al, etc.) critically influence the nature of the oxide scale formed at high temperatures.
Protective oxides such as Al2O3 and Cr2O3, when formed coherently, can significantly slow further oxidation, while volatile or porous oxides (e.g., Mn oxides) lead to spallation.
Microstructural features (e.g., grain boundaries in ultrafine-grained alloys) play a key role in modulating diffusion pathways and thus oxide scale stability.
Parabolic oxidation kinetics and a clear temperature dependence have been consistently observed in these high-entropy systems.

mechanisms: Element-specific diffusion rates controlling cation transport (e.g., fast-diffusing Mn vs. slower Al or Cr) affect which oxide forms at the surface.

Microstructural effects such as grain size and phase distribution modulate effective diffusion coefficients, thereby influencing oxide layer integrity.
The PIP (preferential interactivity parameter) framework explains how local chemistry and nearest-neighbor interactions determine oxidation pathway selection.

open_questions: What is the critical balance of alloying elements in CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) that enables the formation of a stable, coherent protective oxide layer above 900 °C?
How does the introduction of Si, which is less explored in the current literature, influence the competitive oxidation and scale adherence relative to Mn and Al?

opportunities: Combine compositional tuning (e.g., co-alloying with Si and Al) with controlled microstructure engineering to systematically test oxide scale stability.

directions.assessment: By varying X among Si, Mn, and Al in CrFeCoNiX, we can test how the inherent oxidation potentials and diffusion kinetics of each substituent govern the oxide‐scale formation. Prior evidence indicates that Al promotes thin, coherent Al2O3 layers while Mn tends to form porous, unstable Mn‐oxides. Si’s role is less explored but could form silicate/Cr‐oxide mixed layers. This approach directly targets the chemistry-induced balance between protective and non‐protective oxides and is supported by mechanistic models and in situ observations.

Modifying the grain size (ultrafine‐grained vs. coarse-grained) or phase distribution (single-phase vs. multiphase) alters diffusion pathways (especially along grain boundaries) which in turn can accelerate or hinder the formation of coherent protective oxide layers. Evidence from ultrafine-grained HEAs shows improved oxidation resistance and reduced oxide thickness, which underpins the potential of this approach. It directly intervenes on the oxidation kinetics mechanism.

directions.direction: Thermomechanical treatment to modify interfacial stress
directions.assessment: Imposing controlled thermal and mechanical treatments may alter the interfacial stress state between the substrate and the oxide scale by modulating the balance of cation and oxygen diffusion rates. Such treatments could test if a defined balance (reflected in parameters like the PIP) results in compressive stresses that help maintain oxide adhesion. This approach is feasible and mechanistically compelling, though it requires careful in situ stress measurements.

Using the concept of preferential interactivity parameters (PIP) and the Thermo-Oxidative Composition Inversion (TOCI) framework, we can hypothesize that a critical balance between outward cation diffusion (of Cr, Al, or Si) and inward oxygen diffusion governs the formation of a stable, compressively stressed oxide layer. This approach synthesizes existing mechanistic observations and simulations and is testable by correlating diffusion profiles with oxide integrity. It directly addresses the core mechanistic hypothesis regarding oxidizing flux balance.

candidates.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiSi HEA, silicon reacts during high-temperature oxidation to form a continuous interfacial silicate/Cr-oxide mixed layer that effectively accommodates thermal expansion mismatch and reduces interfacial stress, ensuring a stable protective oxide scale above 900 °C; in contrast, the Mn-containing baseline fails to form such a stabilized layer and develops unstable oxide scales.
candidates.intervention: Expose mirror-finished samples to an oxidizing environment (ambient air or 20% O2 in N2) at 900–1050 °C for 24 hours.
candidates.changes: Expanded discussion on the formation and role of an interfacial silicate/Cr-oxide mixed layer. Clarified that silicon contributes by forming silicate species that chemically bond with Cr-oxide to mitigate thermal mismatch. Added references to literature that show similar stabilization in Si-containing alloys.

candidates.hypothesis: In ultrafine-grained CrFeCoNiAl HEA, mechanical processing that refines the grain structure increases grain-boundary density, which accelerates the outward diffusion of protective cations (Cr and Al) to the surface, thereby promoting the rapid formation of a uniform, coherent oxide layer that resists cracking and spallation at 900 °C, in contrast to coarse-grained alloys.
candidates.intervention: Subject both ultrafine-grained and coarse-grained specimens to identical isothermal oxidation at 900 °C in a 20% O2/N2 atmosphere for 24 hours.
candidates.changes: Emphasized and integrated the role of ultrafine-grained structures by citing grain-boundary diffusion studies (e.g., PMC5612997 records) to support enhanced cation transport. Addressed the concern of high-temperature grain growth by suggesting that the ultrafine state be verified pre- and post-exposure.

candidates.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiAl single-phase HEA, the incorporation of aluminum facilitates the rapid formation of a continuous, submicron-thick (≈1 μm) Al2O3-rich protective oxide layer that persists above 900 °C, while a CrFeCoNiMn baseline instead forms thicker, porous, and unstable Mn-rich oxide scales that are prone to cracking and spallation.
candidates.intervention: Expose polished samples to an oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., 20% O2 in N2) at 900–1100 °C for 24 hours.
candidates.changes: Specified quantitative oxide thickness expectations and incorporated supporting literature on Al2O3 formation in Al-containing HEAs (e.g., PMC9692591 and PMC10384371). Addressed review concerns by discussing potential minor phase formation and local segregation effects.
